scenes.tts: Bacteria do not naturally carry a human insulin gene. How can they make human insulin? Before engineered microbes, insulin for patients usually came from cattle and pig pancreases. Then bacteria carrying human instructions began making the medicine.
scenes.caption: Bacteria do not naturally carry a human insulin gene. How can they make human insulin? Before engineered microbes, insulin for patients usually came from cattle and pig pancreases. Then bacteria carrying human instructions began making the medicine.
scenes.visual: Hook first. A large gray bacterium fills the frame while a missing green gene-shaped block pulses above it. Cattle and pig icons slide aside as a medicine vial moves beside the bacterium. Show 'from the 1920s' over the animals and '1982 FDA approval' over the bacterium, only on screen. COLOR MAP for both films: blue = plasmid, green = intended gene or edit, yellow = tools, red = selection or risk, teal = evidence, purple = values. Keep that map throughout. Label noncomputed imagery 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Bacteria do not naturally carry a human insulin gene. How can they make human insulin? Before engineered microbes, insulin for patients usually came from cattle and pig pancreases. Then bacteria carrying human instructions began making the medicine.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: How Bacteria Make Human Insulin. The gray bacterium and missing green block remain faintly visible and drifting behind the title.

scenes.tts: Start with D N A that codes for insulin. Nearly all living things use the same genetic code. But most human genes contain introns, stretches human cells cut out and bacteria cannot. A bacterium can read intron-free D N A for a human protein when bacterial control D N A is present. The gene is the instruction; the control tab helps the bacterium start reading it.
scenes.caption: Start with DNA that codes for insulin. Nearly all living things use the same genetic code. But most human genes contain introns, stretches human cells cut out and bacteria cannot. A bacterium can read intron-free DNA for a human protein when bacterial control DNA is present. The gene is the instruction; the control tab helps the bacterium start reading it.
scenes.visual: The green insulin-gene block grows to fill most of the frame. Briefly show a natural human gene with gray intron segments; the gray segments fade out, leaving one continuous green block labeled 'intron-free' on screen. A smaller green control tab labeled 'bacterial control DNA' locks onto its left edge. A gray bacterial reader sweeps across the joined blocks, then pauses before making any product. Everything is labeled schematic.
scenes.narration: Start with DNA that codes for insulin. Nearly all living things use the same genetic code. But most human genes contain introns, stretches human cells cut out and bacteria cannot. A bacterium can read intron-free DNA for a human protein when bacterial control DNA is present. The gene is the instruction; the control tab helps the bacterium start reading it.

scenes.tts: A restriction enzyme recognizes a D N A sequence. The yellow tool cuts the green gene and a blue plasmid at matching marks. Many cuts leave single-stranded sticky ends. Their shapes show which pieces can pair. The cuts do not add information. They create pieces that can be rearranged.
scenes.caption: A restriction enzyme recognizes a DNA sequence. The yellow tool cuts the green gene and a blue plasmid at matching marks. Many cuts leave single-stranded sticky ends. Their shapes show which pieces can pair. The cuts do not add information. They create pieces that can be rearranged.
scenes.visual: Carry the green gene into a wide view. A yellow restriction-enzyme shape moves between matching yellow marks on the gene and blue plasmid loop. Each cut opens into large complementary notches labeled sticky ends. No molecular structure is drawn.
scenes.narration: A restriction enzyme recognizes a DNA sequence. The yellow tool cuts the green gene and a blue plasmid at matching marks. Many cuts leave single-stranded sticky ends. scenes.tts: The matching ends meet inside the opened plasmid. D N A ligase seals the gaps. The blue loop now carries the green insulin gene. This is recombinant D N A because D N A from different sources has been joined. The plasmid can copy separately from the bacterium's main chromosome.
scenes.caption: The matching ends meet inside the opened plasmid. DNA ligase seals the gaps. The blue loop now carries the green insulin gene. This is recombinant DNA because DNA from different sources has been joined. The plasmid can copy separately from the bacterium's main chromosome.
scenes.visual: The green block slides into the blue loop. A yellow ligase tool travels around both joins and closes them. The completed blue-and-green loop rotates slowly, filling the frame, while the label recombinant DNA settles beneath it.
scenes.narration: The matching ends meet inside the opened plasmid. DNA ligase seals the gaps. The blue loop now carries the green insulin gene. This is recombinant DNA because DNA from different sources has been joined. The plasmid can copy separately from the bacterium's main chromosome.

scenes.tts: Now change one detail. Predict this. The plasmid carries insulin D N A, but its control tab does not work in bacteria. Will the cell make insulin?
scenes.caption: Now change one detail. Predict this. The plasmid carries insulin DNA, but its control tab does not work in bacteria. Will the cell make insulin?
scenes.visual: Keep the same recombinant plasmid large. Fade a warning stripe across only the green control tab. A gray bacterial reader approaches and stops. Put the question above the objects; nothing reveals the answer yet.
scenes.narration: Now change one detail. Predict this. The plasmid carries insulin DNA, but its control tab does not work in bacteria. Will the cell make insulin?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question and stopped reader. The plasmid turns very slowly; the unreadable control tab pulses without changing color.

scenes.tts: No. Carrying a gene is not enough. The cell must recognize its control D N A and read the gene. Replace the tab with one the bacterium recognizes. Now the reader moves, and a green insulin-product block appears. The instruction was present before, but it could not direct a product.
scenes.caption: No. Carrying a gene is not enough. The cell must recognize its control DNA and read the gene. Replace the tab with one the bacterium recognizes. Now the reader moves, and a green insulin-product block appears. The instruction was present before, but it could not direct a product.
scenes.visual: The striped control tab slides away and a working green tab replaces it. The gray reader crosses the gene. A separate green product block grows from a dotted path and moves toward a collection vial labeled insulin product.
scenes.narration: No. Carrying a gene is not enough. The cell must recognize its control DNA and read the gene. Replace the tab with one the bacterium recognizes. Now the reader moves, and a green insulin-product block appears. The instruction was present before, but it could not direct a product.

scenes.tts: Only some bacteria take up a plasmid. The plasmid usually carries an antibiotic-resistance gene for a selection step. On antibiotic, cells without a plasmid fail to grow. Surviving colonies are enriched for cells carrying one. The resistance marker travels on the plasmid; insulin itself does not provide resistance.

scenes.visual: The recombinant loop enters one of three large gray cells. All move onto a red antibiotic plate. Cells without blue plasmids fade to outlines; the plasmid-bearing cell divides into a growing colony. Do not label cells rejected or extinct.
scenes.narration: Only some bacteria take up a plasmid. The plasmid usually carries an antibiotic-resistance gene for a selection step. On antibiotic, cells without a plasmid fail to grow. scenes.tts: As selected bacteria divide, they copy the plasmid and its added gene. If the gene is switched on, cells make the product. Scientists then purify and process that product into insulin medicine. Each daughter can inherit plasmid copies, so, with selection, the colony keeps the added instruction.

scenes.visual: The surviving cell divides twice while blue-and-green plasmids copy into each daughter. Green product blocks stream through a large schematic purification funnel, then settle into medicine vials. Keep 'if switched on' visible during product formation.

scenes.tts: The moving chain is cut, join, carry, select, and read. Each step supports the next, but none guarantees the final effect. Engineering changes a cell's D N A; test the effects, judge each use separately.
scenes.caption: The moving chain is cut, join, carry, select, and read. Each step supports the next, but none guarantees the final effect. Engineering changes a cell's DNA; test the effects, judge each use separately.
scenes.visual: Transform the carried objects into one left-to-right chain: yellow cut tool, sealed blue-green plasmid, bacterium, red selection plate, green product vial. A teal question mark appears after the vial to set up testing without teasing another film.
